note.text: A prefix is added at the beginning of a word. Negative prefixes such as un-, in-, im-, il-, ir- and dis- can create an opposite or negative meaning, but their choice is lexical: not every prefix can attach to every word. Unhappy, incorrect, impossible, illegal, irregular and dishonest are examples. Check spelling and meaning in a dictionary. A word starting with the same letters need not contain a negative prefix. Do not invent a form simply by choosing the prefix that looks shortest.

sections.heading: Understand the ideas
sections.text: A prefix is added at the beginning of a word. Negative prefixes such as un-, in-, im-, il-, ir- and dis- can create an opposite or negative meaning, but their choice is lexical: not every prefix can attach to every word. Unhappy, incorrect, impossible, illegal, irregular and dishonest are examples. Check spelling and meaning in a dictionary. A word starting with the same letters need not contain a negative prefix. Do not invent a form simply by choosing the prefix that looks shortest.

sections.heading: Apply the ideas locally
sections.text: A club report may describe an incorrect date, an impossible deadline and a dishonest claim. Each prefix forms an established word. Replacing incorrect with uncorrect does not produce the expected standard adjective. The change can affect meaning, so a writer should reread the sentence rather than checking spelling alone.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Identify the base word, try the established negative form and check it in a dictionary. Notice patterns such as im- before some words beginning with p, but do not turn a useful pattern into a universal rule without exceptions. Practise the actual words in context.
